'''Algebraic signal processing''' (ASP) is an emerging area of theoretical [[signal processing]] (SP). In the algebraic theory of signal processing, a set of [[Filter (signal processing)|filter]]s is treated as an (abstract) [[Algebra (ring theory)|algebra]], a set of [[Signal (electrical engineering)|signal]]s is treated as a [[Module (mathematics)|module]] or [[vector space]], and [[convolution]] is treated as an [[algebra representation]]. The advantage of algebraic signal processing is its generality and portability.

== History ==
In the original formulation of algebraic signal processing by Puschel and Moura, the signals are collected in an <math>\mathcal{A}
</math>-module for some algebra <math>\mathcal{A}
</math> of filters, and filtering is given by the action of <math>\mathcal{A}
</math> on the <math>\mathcal{A}
</math>-module.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Puschel |first1=M. |last2=Moura |first2=J. |date=2008 |title=Algebraic Signal Processing Theory: Foundation and 1-D Time |journal=IEEE Transactions on Signal Processing |volume=56 |issue=8 |pages=3572–3585 |doi=10.1109/TSP.2008.925261 |bibcode=2008ITSP...56.3572P |s2cid=206797175 |issn=1053-587X|arxiv=cs/0612077 }}</ref>

== Definitions ==
Let <math>K</math> be a [[Field (mathematics)|field]], for instance the complex numbers, and <math>\mathcal{A}</math> be a <math>K</math>-algebra (i.e. a vector space over <math>K</math> with a binary operation <math>\ast: \mathcal{A} \otimes \mathcal{A} \to \mathcal{A}</math> that is linear in both arguments) treated as a set of filters. Suppose <math>\mathcal{M}</math> is a vector space representing a set signals. A ''representation'' of <math>\mathcal{A}</math> consists of an algebra [[homomorphism]] <math>\rho: \mathcal{A} \to \mathrm{End}(\mathcal{M})</math> where <math>\mathrm{End}(\mathcal{M})</math> is the algebra of linear transformations <math>T: \mathcal{M} \to \mathcal{M}</math> with composition (equivalent, in the finite-dimensional case, to [[matrix multiplication]]). For convenience, we write <math>\rho_{a}</math> for the endomorphism <math>\rho(a)</math>. To be an algebra homomorphism, <math>\rho</math> must not only be a linear transformation, but also satisfy the property<math display="block">\rho_{a \ast b} = \rho_{b}\circ\rho_a \quad \forall a, b \in \mathcal{A}</math>Given a signal <math>x \in \mathcal{M}</math>, ''convolution'' of the signal by a filter <math>a \in \mathcal{A}</math> yields a new signal <math>\rho_a(x)</math>. Some additional terminology is needed from the representation theory of algebras. A subset <math>\mathcal{G} \subseteq \mathcal{A}</math> is said to generate the algebra if every element of <math>\mathcal{A}</math> can be represented as polynomials in the elements of <math>\mathcal{G}</math>. The image of a generator <math>g \in \mathcal{G}</math> is called a ''[[shift operator]].'' In all practically all examples, convolutions are formed as polynomials in <math>\mathrm{End}(\mathcal{M})</math> generated by shift operators. However, this is not necessarily the case for a representation of an arbitrary algebra.

== Examples ==

=== Discrete signal processing ===
In [[Digital signal processing|discrete]] signal processing (DSP), the signal space is the set of complex-valued functions <math>\mathcal{M} = \mathcal{L}^2(\mathbb{Z})</math> with bounded energy (i.e. [[Square-integrable function|square-integrable functions]]). This means the infinite series <math>\sum_{n = -\infty}^{\infty} |(x)_n| < \infty</math> where <math>|\cdot|</math> is the [[modulus of a complex number]].  The shift operator is given by the linear endomorphism <math>(S x)_n = (x)_{n-1}</math>. The filter space is the algebra of polynomials with complex coefficients <math>\mathcal{A} = \mathbb{C}[z^{-1},z]</math> and convolution is given by  <math>\rho_{h} = \sum_{k = -\infty}^{\infty} h_k S^k</math> where <math>h(t) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} h_k z^k</math> is an element of the algebra. Filtering a signal by <math>h</math>, then yields <math>(y)_n = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} h_k x_{n-k}</math> because <math>(S^k x)_n = (x)_{n-k}</math>.

=== Graph signal processing ===
A weighted graph is an undirected [[Graph theory|graph]] <math>\mathcal{G} = (\mathcal{V}, \mathcal{E})</math> with [[Pseudometric space|pseudometric]] on the node set <math>\mathcal{V}</math> written <math>a_{ij}</math>. A graph signal is simply a [[real-valued function]] on the set of nodes of the graph. In graph neural networks, graph signals are sometimes called features. The signal space is the set of all graph signals <math>\mathcal{M} = \R^\mathcal{V}</math> where <math>\mathcal{V}</math> is a set of <math>n = |\mathcal{V}|
</math> nodes in <math>\mathcal{G} = (\mathcal{V}, \mathcal{E})</math>. The filter algebra is the algebra of polynomials in one indeterminate <math>\mathcal{A} = \mathbb{R}[t]</math>. There a few possible choices for a graph shift operator (GSO). The (un)normalized weighted [[adjacency matrix]] of <math>[A]_{ij} = a_{ij}</math> is a popular choice, as well as the (un)normalized [[Laplacian matrix|graph Laplacian]] <math>[L]_{ij} =
\begin{cases}
\sum_{j = 1}^{n}a_{ij} & i = j \\
-a_{ij} & i \neq j
\end{cases}
</math>. The choice is dependent on performance and design considerations. If <math>S
</math> is the GSO, then a graph convolution is the linear transformation  <math>\rho_h = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} h_k S^k
</math> for some <math>h(t) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} h_k z^k</math>, and convolution of a graph signal <math>\mathbf{x}: \mathcal{V} \to \mathbb{R}
</math> by a filter <math>h(t)
</math> yields a new graph signal <math>\mathbf{y} = \left(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} h_k S^k \right) \cdot \mathbf{x}
</math>.

=== Other examples ===
Other mathematical objects with their own proposed signal-processing frameworks are algebraic signal models. These objects include including [[Quiver (mathematics)|quivers]],<ref>{{Cite arXiv |last1=Parada-Mayorga |first1=Alejandro |last2=Riess |first2=Hans |last3=Ribeiro |first3=Alejandro |last4=Ghrist |first4=Robert |date=2020-10-22 |title=Quiver Signal Processing (QSP) |class=eess.SP |eprint=2010.11525}}</ref> [[Graphon|graphons]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ruiz |first1=Luana |last2=Chamon |first2=Luiz F. O. |last3=Ribeiro |first3=Alejandro |date=2021 |title=Graphon Signal Processing |journal=IEEE Transactions on Signal Processing |volume=69 |pages=4961–4976 |doi=10.1109/TSP.2021.3106857 |arxiv=2003.05030 |bibcode=2021ITSP...69.4961R |s2cid=212657497 |issn=1053-587X}}</ref> [[semilattices]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Puschel |first1=Markus |last2=Seifert |first2=Bastian |last3=Wendler |first3=Chris |date=2021 |title=Discrete Signal Processing on Meet/Join Lattices |journal=IEEE Transactions on Signal Processing |volume=69 |pages=3571–3584 |doi=10.1109/TSP.2021.3081036 |arxiv=2012.04358 |bibcode=2021ITSP...69.3571P |s2cid=227736440 |issn=1053-587X}}</ref> [[Fourier transform on finite groups|finite groups]], and [[Lie group|Lie groups]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bernardini |first1=Riccardo |last2=Rinaldo |first2=Roberto |date=2021 |title=Demystifying Lie Group Methods for Signal Processing: A Tutorial |journal=IEEE Signal Processing Magazine |volume=38 |issue=2 |pages=45–64 |doi=10.1109/MSP.2020.3023540 |bibcode=2021ISPM...38b..45B |s2cid=232071730 |issn=1053-5888}}</ref> and others. 

== Intertwining maps ==
In the framework of [[representation theory]], relationships between two representations of the same algebra are described with [[Equivariant map|intertwining maps]] which in the context of signal processing translates to transformations of signals that respect the algebra structure. Suppose <math>\rho: \mathcal{A} \to \mathrm{End}(\mathcal{M})</math> and <math>\rho': \mathcal{A} \to \mathrm{End}(\mathcal{M}')</math> are two different representations of <math>\mathcal{A}</math>. An ''intertwining map'' is a linear transformation <math>\alpha: \mathcal{M} \to \mathcal{M}'</math> such that

<math>\alpha \circ \rho_a =  \rho'_a \circ \alpha \quad \forall a \in \mathcal{A}</math>

Intuitively, this means that filtering a signal by <math>a</math> then transforming it with <math>\alpha</math> is equivalent to first transforming a signal with <math>\alpha
</math>, then filtering by <math>a</math>. The [[z transform]]<ref name=":0" /> is a  prototypical example of an intertwining map.  

== Algebraic neural networks ==
Inspired by a recent perspective that popular graph neural networks (GNNs) architectures are in fact [[Convolutional neural network|convolutional neural networks]] (CNNs),<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Gama |first1=Fernando |last2=Isufi |first2=Elvin |last3=Leus |first3=Geert |last4=Ribeiro |first4=Alejandro |date=2020 |title=Graphs, Convolutions, and Neural Networks: From Graph Filters to Graph Neural Networks |journal=IEEE Signal Processing Magazine |volume=37 |issue=6 |pages=128–138 |doi=10.1109/MSP.2020.3016143 |arxiv=2003.03777 |bibcode=2020ISPM...37f.128G |s2cid=226292855 |issn=1053-5888}}</ref> recent work has been focused on developing novel neural network architectures from the algebraic point-of-view.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Parada-Mayorga |first1=Alejandro |last2=Ribeiro |first2=Alejandro |date=2021 |title=Algebraic Neural Networks: Stability to Deformations |journal=IEEE Transactions on Signal Processing |volume=69 |pages=3351–3366 |doi=10.1109/TSP.2021.3084537 |arxiv=2009.01433 |bibcode=2021ITSP...69.3351P |s2cid=221517145 |issn=1053-587X}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Parada-Mayorga |first1=Alejandro |last2=Butler |first2=Landon |last3=Ribeiro |first3=Alejandro |date=2023 |title=Convolutional Filtering and Neural Networks with Non Commutative Algebras |journal=IEEE Transactions on Signal Processing |volume=71 |page=2683 |doi=10.1109/TSP.2023.3293716 |arxiv=2108.09923|bibcode=2023ITSP...71.2683P }}</ref> An algebraic neural network is a composition of algebraic convolutions, possibly with multiple features and feature aggregations, and nonlinearities.
